newsitem.title: USA: Communication problem stops Mars rover deployment.
newsitem.headline: Communication problem stops Mars rover deployment.

text.p: Space officials worked on Saturday to fix a communications problem with the Pathfinder spacecraft and salvage a $266 million scientific mission to Mars.
Unless the problem can be solved, mission control will be unable to deploy the Sojourner rover that was built to explore part of the Martian surface analysing rock and soil samples.

If full communications cannot be established, the rover will carry out some nominal pre-programmed tasks, but no scientific data can be relayed back to Earth, officials of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) said.

The problem was also thwarting attempts to get the rover to roll down a ramp off the lander to the surface of Mars. The operation was held up because one of the airbags deployed to cushion Pathfiner's landing had not fully deflated.

The glitches overshadowed what had been a picture-book landing of Pathfinder on Friday after travelling 309 million miles (497 million km) since it blasted off from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Dec. 4 last year.

Rover manager Jake Matijevic told reporters at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory that the communications problem was essentially a software problem involving the modem linking Sojourner to the Pathfinder lander.
"We believe the modem survived the landing," he said. "Either communication works or it does not, but we have never seen anything like this.

"Only the shortest frames of communications are getting through," he said, explaining that his team was sending short command sequences to try to reset the rover's system. But they would not know until later in the day if they were successful.

"We have degraded communications -- only one syllable instead of full sentences," Brian Muirhead, flight system manager and deputy Pathfinder project manager, said. "(But) I am confident we'll get to the bottom of the problem."
Until the communications problem is corrected, the $25 million rover remains sitting on the lander, unable to respond to signals to roll down the ramp onto the surface of Mars.

After two days, Matijevic said, Sojourner would begin to respond to pre-programmed signals. It would assess its position and condition and roll down the ramp to begin analysing rock samples. But mission control would not be able to direct it and any scientific data would not be transmitted back to Earth.

But Muirhead rejected suggestions that this would amount to a scientific failure for the first landing on Mars since the Viking mission 21 years ago. "We're still 90 percent successful. The goal of the mission was to land a craft on Mars and send back images," he said.
"Of course we'll be very disapointed," he said, when asked about the possibility of communications not being restored. "We want to see the rover roll off."
His frustration was shared by project scientist Matt Golombek, who told reporters: "There are all sorts of things out there we are dying to go look at."

If the rover performs only "nominal operations," Sojourner will move only 3-5 yards (metres) from the lander. "It can go on for some time, but the only information we could get back would be the imaging," Matijevic said.

The images Pathfinder has already sent back to Earth were spectacular, however. Peter Smith, head of the imaging team, said Pathfinder landed in the area known as Ares Vallis, about 2-3 miles (3-4 km) from a large crater.

Pointing out rocks and other objects on computer-enhanced pictures, including one peak on the horizon about 20 miles (32 km) away, Smith brought laughs from the audience when he noted one curiously shaped image.
"The most mysterious object looks like a couch," he said, joking that maybe there was a homeless person on Mars.
At first his colleagues thought it was the parachute that had helped bring Pathfinder through the Martian atmosphere, he said, but that was brightly coloured and this object was not.
